title.en: Exploring the investigative world of science

text.en: Meera watches puris puff in hot oil and wonders: why do some puff well and some do not? To find out, she must investigate like a scientist.

Science begins with curiosity: we observe, ask questions and look for explanations.
This year's journey goes from tiny microbes we cannot see to planet-wide challenges like climate change.
Watching the Moon's phases helped humans make the first calendars, which links our daily routine to objects beyond Earth.
A scientific investigation starts with a question, then a guess called a hypothesis, then a fair test, then observations and a conclusion.
In a fair test we change only one thing at a time, such as the thickness of dough, and keep every other condition the same.
We should note everything we see, smell and sense, such as whether the oil splattered or smoked.
Measuring carefully and repeating the experiment make our results more reliable.
A result can raise new questions, such as whether fresh dough puffs better than stored dough, and that is how science grows.
Scientific principles of observing, measuring and experimenting also help us understand problems like climate change.
Safety first: always follow the teacher's instructions and handle materials carefully in any investigation.

problem.en: Plan a fair test for: does thicker dough puff less?

text.en: Question: Does the thickness of the dough change how much a puri puffs?
Change only the thickness; keep oil temperature, size and cooking time the same.
Measure the height of each puri and repeat three times.

prompt.en: Why must a fair test change only one thing?

requiredIdeas.en: Otherwise we cannot tell which change caused the result.
Other conditions are kept the same.

points.en: Science starts with observation and questions.
A fair test changes only one variable.
